at.deep: Production failures this topic warns about

items.item: A deterministic transform (output from input alone) and an idempotent write (repetition has no further effect) together, not separately, are what make a re-run trustworthy.

at.step: Reveal: deterministic transforms and idempotent writes

items.item: A hidden non-determinism (wall-clock time, input ordering, an unseeded sample) can make two runs over identical input silently disagree, with no data having changed.

at.step: Predict: which hidden non-determinism caused the disagreement?

items.item: A watermark is a heuristic assertion that input is complete up to a point in time, not a guarantee — late events are the expected cost of that heuristic being wrong sometimes.

at.step: Reveal: the watermark and late events

items.item: A correction window turns a late event from something dropped or silently overwritten into something that amends a published result with a new version.

at.step: Reveal: the correction window amends, instead of dropping or corrupting

items.item: A correction window's width is set by a measured late-data rate and is a real cost in held state and consumer-visible change, not a free margin.

at.step: Reveal: sizing the window from the late-data rate

items.item: A versioned output lets a consumer pin a version and an auditor reconstruct exactly what was reported and when, by appending rather than overwriting.

at.step: Reveal: versioned outputs

items.item: Pipeline-level determinism and idempotence don't automatically protect an external side effect (an email, a webhook) — that needs its own deduplication key.

at.step: Prove it

items.item: This topic leaves out watermark generation, trigger mechanics, Kafka/Flink delivery recipes, the exactly-once argument, and table-format snapshot mechanics deliberately — it teaches the design response, not the mechanics.
Deterministic, idempotent pipeline design and watermark-based lateness handling are established, Dataflow-Model-era practice, not an emerging technique.

This topic fixes the shop's own replay-correctness and late-data design that the next topic (failure-mode analysis and recovery) assumes already holds before asking what happens when a component is simply down.
